extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students interested in history of mathematics / numeration
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting the criteria by which historical and modern numeration systems (and counting devices) can be judged — e.g., positional principle, symbol for empty class, compactness, ease of calculation, mechanical compatibility, and cultural acceptance. Useful for comparing cardinal, ordinal, and positional systems and for understanding why the Hindu-Arabic system prevailed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cardinal principle (stroke-based numerals and class symbols)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each numeral up to nine is merely a collection of strokes. Units of a higher class, such as tens, hundreds, etc., are represented by special symbols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Found in cuneiform, Egyptian, and early Chinese records; contrasts with ordinal systems that use alphabetic letters. The text emphasizes this as the 'distinctly cardinal character' of the earliest records and illustrates with tallies and notches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordinal numeration (alphabetic/ordinal principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinal numeration represents numbers by the letters of an alphabet in their spoken succession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exemplified by Phoenician, Hebrew, and early Greek numerations; arose from desire for compactness in commerce and was adopted with the alphabet itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability for arithmetical operations / ease of calculation
rubrics_metrics.description: How well is the system adopted to arithmetical operations, and what ease does it lend to calculations?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter explicitly poses this as a central question: compact recording is not enough — the key is whether the system facilitates calculation. It argues Greek ordinal and Roman systems were 'not capable of creating an arithmetic which could be used by a man of average intelligence,' and medieval rules for operating on such numerals were complex and cumbersome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of position (positional numeration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Giving the numeral a value which depends not only on the digit but on the position it occupies relative to other symbols of the group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained with examples (342 = 3 hundreds + 4 tens + 2 units) and linked to the counting-board scheme; presented as the pivotal discovery enabling simple, general rules for arithmetic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbol for an empty class (zero / empty column)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is essential to have some method of representing the gaps, i.e., a symbol for an empty column — a symbol for nothing (zero).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without such a symbol a written record of a counting-board operation is ambiguous (e.g., === could represent 32, 302, 320, 3002, etc.). The text traces the linguistic and conceptual evolution from Indian sunya ('empty') to Arabic sifr and Latin/Italian forms, emphasizing that invention of a zero-symbol was a prerequisite for positional notation to be practical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unambiguity for permanent records
rubrics_metrics.description: A numeration must permit an unambiguous permanent record of counting-board operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tied to the need for a zero/empty-column symbol; the lack of such led to ambiguities that prevented transitioning counting-board methods into reliable written numerals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compactness of notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Compactness of notation — the ability to record numbers succinctly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter notes compactness as a driving motivation (e.g., Phoenician adoption) and later cites 'compactness of its notation' as one of the advantages of positional numeration that should have assured its acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algorithmic amenability (algorism / algorithm)
rubrics_metrics.description: The system should support systematic procedures (algorithms) for calculations — i.e., stepwise rules that operate on results of previous steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically 'algorithm' (algorism) was synonymous with positional numeration; the chapter references Al-Khwarizmi and explains that algorithmic procedures are central to arithmetical practice and transmission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compatibility with mechanical counting devices (abacus and counters)
rubrics_metrics.description: How naturally the written numeration corresponds to mechanical devices like counting boards/abaci, where columns represent decimal classes and counters record unit counts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text repeatedly compares counting-board representation with written numerals and shows that positional notation is essentially a translation of the counting-board scheme; it also describes varieties of abaci and the roles of counters versus written marks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessibility to the average person / democratization of arithmetic
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the numeration makes arithmetic accessible to the average person rather than requiring specialists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argued emphatically: prior numerations made computation the province of experts; positional numeration 'did away with these obstacles and made arithmetic accessible even to the dullest mind.' This criterion ties directly to measured social impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptability to the growing complexities of commerce, industry, and administration
rubrics_metrics.description: The numeration must meet the computational demands arising from commerce, taxation, military organization, land/property accounting, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter points out that growing societal complexities called for calculations beyond finger-technique and clumsy numerations, motivating mechanical devices and ultimately the positional system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representational stability (standardized numeral shapes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stability and standardization of numeral shapes so that notation becomes consistent across users and time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text observes that numeral shapes 'did not assume a stable form until the introduction of printing' and that printing had a 'stabilizing influence' so modern numerals resemble those of the fifteenth century.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural, political, and institutional acceptance (resistance and costs of adoption)
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree to which tradition, legal prohibitions, institutional inertia, and public attitude influence adoption of a numeration system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes the long struggle between Abacists and Algorists (11th–15th centuries), bans on Arabic numerals, 'bootlegging' use by merchants, legal prohibitions, and anecdotes (e.g., parliamentary tally-sticks) showing how non-technical factors delayed adoption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foundational role for further mathematical development
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the system paves the way to generalized number concepts and other mathematical advances (e.g., algebra).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter links the discovery of positional notation and zero to the rise of a generalized number concept and algebra, noting that both positional numeration and algebra originated in India and that without positional notation no progress in arithmetic (and hence many branches of mathematics) would have been possible.
